Acrylic paint-along · beginner

A small red sailboat with white sails on calm teal water at sunset, with a purple hill and a low far shore under an orange and violet sky.

Start on a plain white canvas. Paint the sky first, then each part of the scene from farthest to nearest, each straight over the one behind it. Then the main subject, texture with simple brush moves, shadows, and highlights last.

8 stepsFocal point: The red sailboat at the right (hull 68% to 86% across, 57% to 63% down; mast top 26% down at 76% across). Light: The setting sun, low and just left of center (48% across, 42% down). It lights the sky gold around it and lays a broken gold path down the water below it.How this lesson was made

What you need

Tubes

  • Titanium white
  • Cadmium yellow medium (hue)
  • Cadmium red medium (hue)
  • Ultramarine blue
  • Burnt sienna

Brushes

  • 1 inch flat: covering and blending the whole skyFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • #8 round: the sun diskRound: pointed tip, thin or thick depending on how hard you press
  • #10 flat: the hill and the shore bandFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • #6 flat: short dashes of light on the waterFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • #4 round: the sails' edges and fillRound: pointed tip, thin or thick depending on how hard you press
  • Liner (#1 or #0): the mast, boom, and hull trimLiner: long, very thin bristles, for fine lines like twigs and grass

Also

  • White canvas or canvas board
  • Water jar and paper towel
  • Palette or paper plate for mixing

Every paint in the lesson. You don't have to mix them all at the start: each step lists the paints it uses with their recipes, so you can mix a little as you go before it dries. Parts are by volume.

The steps

Step 1Step 2Step 3Step 4Step 5Step 6Step 7Step 8

STEP 1 OF 8

Blend the sunset sky

  1. The light comes from the sun, low and just left of center. Every highlight faces it.
  2. With the 1 inch flat and creamy Twilight violet, pull long side-to-side strokes across the top tenth.
  3. X-stroke Sunset pink below it, then Sunset orange down to a straight line about 55% down. The water covers the bottom later.
  4. While wet, X-stroke Glow gold just left of center above that line, and Sunset pink along the sky's bottom. Smooth joins with long strokes; stop when it drags.
  5. Done: violet, pink, orange, a gold glow, white canvas below.
Paints for this step4 paints, 4 new
  • Twilight violet new3 parts ultramarine, 3 parts white, 1 part red
  • Sunset pink new1 part red, 1 part white, a touch of ultramarine
  • Sunset orange new3 parts red, 2 parts yellow, 2 parts white
  • Glow gold new3 parts yellow, 3 parts white, 2 parts red

Brushes

1 inch flat

Strokes

Long horizontal blend. Pull the flat side to side in long, level strokes for the violet band.

X stroke. Criss-cross the flat in overlapping X shapes to lay in and blend the pink, orange, and gold.

Watch out: Colors dry a little darker: test each mix on the palette edge first.

Watch out: Work fast; the whole sky is one wet blend of about 5 minutes.

Heads up, this picture is a little off: The sky stops at about 54% down, right at the horizon, not 60% as planned, so it doesn't run past the shore line. Spotted after the review (round 1 found no issues). Paint what the steps say.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 2 OF 8

Paint the sun

  1. Let the sky dry.
  2. With the #8 round and creamy Sun cream, fill a thumbnail-sized circle in small circles, just left of center, a little above the sky's bottom edge.
  3. Let it dry and give it a second coat so the orange doesn't show through.
  4. Done: a pale round sun in the gold glow.
Paints for this step1 paint, 1 new
  • Sun cream new6 parts white, 3 parts yellow, 1 part red

Brushes

#8 round

Strokes

Small circles with the brush tip. Turn the tip in small circles from the middle out, so the edge stays soft and round.

Watch out: Keep the circle round: turn the canvas if that helps.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 3 OF 8

Paint the hill and the far shore

  1. Let the sky dry.
  2. With the #10 flat and creamy Hill purple, start at the left edge a little below the sun, rise to a rounded top a fifth across, then slope down to just right of the sun.
  3. With Shore navy, pull a thin, level band across the whole canvas just under the hill.
  4. Mix a little Hill purple into Sunset pink and paint a low, soft ridge on the shore from just right of the sun to the right edge.
  5. Done: hill, far ridge, and shore over the sky, white canvas below.
Paints for this step2 paints, 2 new
  • Hill purple new2 parts ultramarine, 1 part burnt sienna, 1 part white
  • Shore navy new3 parts ultramarine, 1 part burnt sienna, 1 part white

Brushes

#10 flat

Strokes

Curved strokes that follow a form. Follow the hill's slope with the flat so the strokes curve over its top.

Horizontal strokes for flat ground. Keep the brush level and pull long strokes for the shore band.

Watch out: Keep the hill plain and soft; far things get no detail.

Watch out: Keep the shore's bottom edge level: it's the horizon.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 4 OF 8

Paint the calm water

  1. Let the shore dry.
  2. With the 1 inch flat and creamy Light teal, pull long horizontal strokes from just under the shore line down about a third of the water.
  3. Load Deep teal and keep going to the bottom edge, blending into the lighter teal while wet.
  4. While it's wet, skim the brush corner with Light teal in short, level, broken streaks: more near the shore, fewer and wider lower down.
  5. Done: rippled teal water, lighter near the shore, no white canvas left.
Paints for this step2 paints, 2 new
  • Light teal new3 parts ultramarine, 2 parts white, 1 part yellow
  • Deep teal new3 parts ultramarine, 1 part yellow, 1 part white

Deep teal is as close as these tubes get; it mixes a little grayer than the picture.

Brushes

1 inch flat

Strokes

Long horizontal blend. Pull level side-to-side strokes all the way across, overlapping each one a little.

Watch out: Keep every stroke level, or the water will look like it slopes.

Watch out: Paint right over where the reflections go; they come later.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 5 OF 8

Paint the sun's reflection

  1. Let the water dry.
  2. With the #6 flat and creamy Sunset orange, tap short level dashes straight below the sun, shore to near the bottom, wider and farther apart going down.
  3. With Sun cream, add dashes down the middle, about four-fifths of the way, leaving orange at each side.
  4. With the flat's corner, add a few tiny orange dashes to each side, and thin glints just under the shore.
  5. Done: a broken gold path, teal between the dashes.
Paints for this step2 paints

  • Sun cream from step 2, mix more if it has dried6 parts white, 3 parts yellow, 1 part red

Orange over teal may need a second coat once the first dries.

Brushes

#6 flat

Strokes

Horizontal strokes for flat ground. Touch the flat down and pull a short level dash, then lift. Try a few on scrap paper first.

Watch out: Leave teal between the dashes; it's a broken path, not a stripe.

Watch out: This is the ugly stage for many painters. It's normal; keep going.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 6 OF 8

Block in the boat

  1. Let the water and sky dry.
  2. With the #6 flat and creamy Boat red, paint the hull: from two-thirds across to about an eighth from the right edge, just under the shore line. Straight top, curved bottom, pointed right end.
  3. With the #4 round and Sail white, paint two triangles on the hull, sharing one upright edge three-quarters across. Their tops reach a quarter of the way down; the right one is wider.
  4. Let it dry and give the sails a second coat. Done: flat red hull, white sails.

Brushes

#6 flat#4 round

Strokes

Building from pieces. Paint the hull as one long shape first, then the two sails as triangles standing on it.

Watch out: White over orange needs two or three coats; let each dry.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 7 OF 8

Add the mast, boom, and trim

  1. Let the boat dry.
  2. With the liner and Mast brown thinned like ink, pull one straight line up the edge where the sails meet, from the hull to the sails' top.
  3. Pull a short line along the bottom of the right sail for the boom.
  4. With Sail white, run a thin line along the top of the hull. With the #6 flat, stroke Boat red darkened with Mast brown along the hull's bottom. Done: the boat is finished.

Brushes

Liner (#1 or #0)

Strokes

Liner work. Hold the liner upright and pull with light, steady pressure in one go.

Watch out: Try a liner line on scrap paper first; reload often so it doesn't skip.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 8 OF 8

Paint the boat's reflection

  1. Let the water dry.
  2. With the #6 flat and Boat red, pull short horizontal strokes just under the hull, as wide as the hull.
  3. Below that, add wavy horizontal dashes of Sail white, narrowing as they go down, about as far as the sun's path reaches.
  4. Let the white dry. With the liner and thinned Mast brown, wiggle a line down the middle of it. Done: the finished painting.

How Claude read your photosubject, light, layers

Before starting

Subject: a red sailboat on calm water at sunset

Found in the image: just the picture

Done: none

Why: No bars, borders, captions, or page around it.

Beginner version

What made it too busy: No tiny separate things besides the boat, which is the subject. No textures of hundreds of items (the reflections are a few dozen dashes). No detail inside big shapes. Eight parts, within max_parts 8.

Changed: none

Why: The picture was made beginner-sized, so the photo was used as is.

A calm sunset seascape made to be simple: a violet-to-orange sky with the sun, one purple hill, a thin far shore, teal water with the sun's broken reflection, and a small red sailboat with its reflection. What matters is a clean sky blend, level water, and a crisp little boat. The hard parts are white sails over orange (several coats) and keeping reflections broken.

Subject: A small red sailboat with white sails on calm teal water at sunset, with a purple hill and a low far shore under an orange and violet sky.

How the paint recipes were worked out12 paints, free

Paint doesn't mix like light on a screen: blue and yellow make green, not gray. So the recipes come from a pigment mixing model (Mixbox), not a guess. For each paint it tried every simple recipe from your tubes, up to three colors plus white, and kept the one that lands closest to the color in the painting. Delta E is how far off it lands: under 2 is hard to see, under 5 is close, and over 8 means these tubes can't quite make it.

Why the steps go in this order8 steps

Back to front: the sky, the sun in it, the hill and shore over the sky, the water below, the sun's reflection on the dry water, then the boat (flat shapes, then the mast and trim), and its reflection last. Eight steps for eight parts; nothing was split because no part has dense texture.

  1. 1. Blend the sunset sky

    Every layer sits on the sky, and it's one wet blend, so it goes first.

  2. 2. Paint the sun

    Light over the dry orange needs its own step and two coats.

  3. 3. Paint the hill and the far shore

    The farthest land, at one distance, so one step.

  4. 4. Paint the calm water

    The biggest area after the sky; reflections need it dry underneath.

  5. 5. Paint the sun's reflection

    Light dashes over the dry water, before the boat goes on top.

  6. 6. Block in the boat

    The subject after its background; flat shapes first, as the technique asks.

  7. 7. Add the mast, boom, and trim

    Liner lines go over dry paint, so the boat's details get their own step.

  8. 8. Paint the boat's reflection

    The reflection sits under the finished boat and ends the painting.

What Claude would do differentlyfor the next lesson
  • The research notes have no section on water or reflections (broken horizontal dashes, reflections narrowing downward). This lesson leaned on the YAML's horizontal-strokes entry and the picture.
  • Seam-free water patching needs more than a copied strip: both throwaway tries left seams. A filter that fills from rows on both sides with texture synthesis could make 'remove a reflection on plain water' free.
  • Step renders stopped the sky at the horizon (54%) even though looks_like asked for 60%; the painter's text says to run it past.
  • Skill gap: SKILL.md asks for each instruction under about 35 words, but publish's long_steps only checks a step's total (110 words), so a long single instruction isn't flagged.
  • The plan missed the faint far ridge right of the sun; the step review caught it. When the finish has a low soft shape behind the main one, list it as a component.
